youtube.why: On a double-paired board the jam is a full house far too often; people don't bluff here.
A check-jam over a pot-size bet on A-K-Q is massively under-bluffed; a bluffer would just bet.
Check-call, check-call, then a big lead is under-bluffed, and he has no missed draws to bluff with.
After a check-raise and a turn barrel, the jam is never a bluff: AT always, KQ sometimes.
Recreational players don't overbet as a bluff on this board; exploit fold.
Recs slowplay big flushes on monotone boards and don't check-raise all in with small ones or bluffs.
Smaller flushes don't check-raise a big turn bet, so this is only the nut or second-nut flush.
Nobody bluff-raises the turn in a 3-bet pot after you bet every street; just fold every time.
Turn and river raises at low stakes are almost never bluffs, even at a great price.
He won't donk two pair or a set this way, and we gave no rope, so it's a ten almost every time.
He calls his own fold pretty bad: after the turn check-back his pair is a fine bluff catcher on a clean river.
Recs reach the river too wide; half pot is their bluff size, value would bet bigger.
The CO stabbed last to act, so his range is wide; small size, good price, we gave rope.
When low-stakes players pick more than 60% pot on the river they just always have it.
A rec who 3-bets the small blind and fires three times is under-bluffed; calling the turn doesn't commit you.
Draws missed and won't call anything, so bet small to get called by 8x and 9x.
This player never folds a king, so bet big on the turn to get value from Kx and draws.
Against a sticky player who never folds a king, just jam.
Ask how much it takes to fold an ace: egregiously large. $85 was far too small.
Out of position at low SPR, minimise streets and jam: QQ, JJ and TT can't fold.
A small or thin value bet on the ace was better than checking.
A fish won't double-barrel his overpairs, so lead a size he calls with them.
Set up by the turn lead: jam the river.
A9 and A5 play this way too; you need about 30% and have 10 outs against two pair.
With two fish between you and the reg raiser, donk: the reg won't stab 4-way, so target the fish.

youtube.why: Size the turn so the river jam is about half the pot.
Fish rarely jam their flushes for you, so jam yourself.
The flop checked through, so both ranges are capped: check-raise the delayed c-bet as a bluff.
Keep bluffing when the flush comes; a big size folds AJ.
His best hand is weak Ax; to make AT call he'd bet 400-450, so the jam folds it.
The turn check-raise looks very strong: jam and about 90% of his range folds, every Ax included.
$410 isn't scary enough for a sticky player: go egregious, about 4x pot, to fold his whole range.
His check-calls say overpair, few flushes; a big overbet folds TT-JJ.
Small in-position river bets are thin value; a big raise folds AT and KT.
His turn stab is mostly Ax; check-raise small so AJ and AT call once.
Then overbet the river to fold them; he has almost no strong hands.
Regs bet this turn too thin and know live check-raises are rarely bluffs, so they fold.
